newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Clinton hails U.N., says most Americans support it.
newsitem.headline: Clinton hails U.N., says most Americans support it.

text.p: President Bill Clinton paid a glowing tribute to the United Nations on Tuesday, saying the vast majority of Americans supported the organisation and promising to pay owed dues amounting to some $1.6 billion.
"In this time of challenge and change, the United Nations is more important than ever because our world is more interdependent than ever," he told the General Assembly.

Most Americans knew this, although "unfortunately, some Americans -- in their longing to be free of the world's problems and their pre-occupation with our own -- ignore our interdependence and the benefits of cooperation," he said.

They ignored all the United Nations was doing to improve millions of lives by preserving peace, vaccinating children, caring for refugees and sharing the blessings of progress around the world, he said.

"They have made it difficult for the United States to meet its financial obligations to the U.N.," he continued, alluding to hostility towards the world body, particularly among the Republican majority in the U.S. Congress.
Some extremist groups even accuse the United Nations of seeking to take over the United States and claim to have sighted sinister black U.N. helicopters flying over various parts of the country.

Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, whose hopes for a second five-year term the United States has threatened to veto if necessary, was seated on the rostrum behind Clinton as he addressed the 185-member Assembly. Washington says the world body needs new leadership to carry out sweeping reforms.

When the president arrived at U.N. headquarters, he and the secretary-general exchanged cordial greetings and a handshake against the backdrop of U.S. and U.N. flags. They conferred briefly -- mainly about African problems, a U.N. spokesman said -- before Clinton became the first world leader to sign the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban treaty and then addressed the Assembly.
In his speech, he said the "vast majority of Americans support the United Nations -- not only because it reflects our ideals, but because it reinforces our interests."

The United States would be the largest financial contributor to the U.N. system for the 51st year, he said, adding: "We are paying our dues and we are committed to paying off our accrued obligations soon."
The approximately $1.6 billion owed by the United States accounts for more than half the $2.8 billion in unpaid dues for the regular U.N. budget and U.N. peacekeeping operations.

Clinton said the United Nations was committed to a "reform process that is streamlining operations, reining in its budget, and readying the U.N. for the demands of the new century. And it must continue."
